An inland rail port on the border of Kazakhstan and Chinese Xinjiang, opened in 2015. It lies near the twin towns both called Khorgos, about 200 km from the old Dzungarian Gate pass.

Its job is to fix a mismatch. China lays its tracks at standard gauge, while Kazakhstan and the rest of the former Soviet Union use a wider gauge. At Khorgos, cranes lift containers from one train to another, so freight can run from Chinese factories to Europe in two to three weeks, far faster than by sea.

The port is a showpiece of China's Belt and Road Initiative, which pays for roads, rails and pipes across Central Asia. A free trade zone straddles the border next to it. In a sense it revives the role of the Silk Road caravan towns, with trains in place of camels.
